metric_identity.metric_name: AI Training Cost Reduction Curve — Multidimensional decline in the cost to train and run AI systems, encompassing hardware cost per FLOP, algorithmic efficiency, and inference cost per unit of performance
metric_identity.source_report: Composite metric drawing primarily from: (1) Stanford HAI AI Index Report 2025 (280x inference cost reduction), (2) Epoch AI 'Trends in the Dollar Training Cost of Machine Learning Systems' (2024), (3) ARK Invest 'AI Training Costs Are Improving at 50x the Speed of Moore's Law' (2024), (4) OpenAI 'AI and Efficiency' (2020)
metric_identity.publication_date: April 2025 (Stanford HAI); ongoing updates (Epoch AI); February 2024 (ARK Invest)
metric_identity.methodology_notes: Multiple measurement approaches converge on the same conclusion. Stanford HAI/Epoch AI measured the API price per million tokens to achieve a fixed benchmark score (MMLU 64.8%, equivalent to GPT-3.5 performance) over time, tracking from $20.00/M tokens (Nov 2022) to $0.07/M tokens (Oct 2024, Gemini-1.5-Flash-8B). ARK Invest measured the public cloud cost to train a specific model (ResNet-50 on ImageNet) to a fixed accuracy, tracking from ~$1,000 (2017) to ~$10 (2019) to ~$4.60 (2021) — a 223x reduction. Epoch AI separately tracks the dollar training cost of frontier models, which paradoxically increases (3.5x/year since 2020) because frontier labs push capability boundaries. The 280x figure specifically measures inference cost to reach a fixed performance level, not frontier training cost.

metric_value.value: 280x reduction in inference cost for GPT-3.5-level performance (Nov 2022 to Oct 2024). Additionally: 223x reduction in ResNet-50 training cost (2017-2021); hardware cost per FLOP declined ~74% from 2019-2025 (2025 price per FP32 FLOP is ~26% of the 2019 price); algorithmic efficiency doubles every ~16 months (halving compute required for equivalent performance); ARK Invest reports training costs dropping ~10x per year, 50x faster than Moore's Law. DeepSeek V3 trained for $5.6M vs GPT-4's estimated $78M-$100M.
metric_value.unit: Multiple: fold-reduction (280x), USD per million tokens ($20.00 to $0.07), USD training cost ($1,000 to $4.60 for ResNet-50), cost halving time (months)
metric_value.time_period: 2017-2025 (broad trend); November 2022 to October 2024 (280x inference figure)
metric_value.comparison_baseline: Inference: $20.00 per million tokens for GPT-3.5-level MMLU performance in November 2022. Training: ~$1,000 to train ResNet-50 on public cloud in 2017. Frontier model training: GPT-4 estimated at $78M (Stanford HAI) to $100M.
metric_value.market_layer: cross-cutting (covers infrastructure hardware costs, model training efficiency, and application-layer inference pricing)

trend.year_over_year_change: Inference cost per unit of fixed performance: declining 9x-900x per year depending on task and benchmark (Epoch AI), with a median of ~50x per year. Hardware cost per FLOP: declining ~30% annually. Algorithmic efficiency: compute required halves every ~16 months. Training cost for fixed tasks (e.g., ResNet-50): ~10x per year decline. Frontier model absolute training costs: increasing ~3.5x per year (countervailing trend).
trend.compound_annual_growth_rate: Cost decline CAGR varies by layer: hardware cost per FLOP ~-30%/year; algorithmic efficiency ~-50%/16 months; combined training cost for fixed benchmarks: ~-90%/year (ARK Invest); inference price for GPT-3.5-level: ~-99.6% over 18 months
trend.forecast_value: ARK Invest projects training costs to decline 75% annually through 2030 (combining 53%/year hardware improvement and 47%/year algorithmic gains). If inference cost decline continues at 50x/year (Epoch AI median), GPT-4-level inference could cost under $0.01 per million tokens by 2026-2027.
trend.velocity_indicator: cost_halving_time: Inference cost for fixed performance halves roughly every 2-4 months (derived from 50x/year median). Hardware cost per FLOP halves every ~2.5 years for GPUs. Algorithmic efficiency compute requirement halves every ~16 months. For hard coding tasks specifically, inference costs halve roughly every 2 months.

entrepreneurial_relevance.relevance_for_entrepreneurs: This is arguably the most important economic trend for AI startup founders to understand. The 280x cost reduction in 18 months means: (1) Business models that were unit-economics-negative a year ago may now be highly profitable — founders should continuously re-evaluate which AI-powered products become viable as costs crater; (2) The cost curve is moving so fast that pricing strategies built on today's inference costs will be obsolete within months — build margin structures that benefit from deflation, not ones that depend on current prices; (3) DeepSeek V3 training at $5.6M vs GPT-4's ~$80M demonstrates that frontier model training is becoming accessible to well-funded startups, not just hyperscalers — the barrier to entry for custom model development is falling rapidly; (4) The divergence between falling per-unit costs and rising frontier absolute costs creates a two-tier market: commodity-grade intelligence becomes nearly free, while cutting-edge capabilities remain expensive — startups should decide which tier they compete in; (5) For European/French founders specifically, falling training costs reduce the disadvantage of not having hyperscaler-scale compute budgets, potentially enabling competitive models from organizations like Mistral AI at a fraction of US costs.
entrepreneurial_relevance.actionable_insight: Design products assuming inference costs will drop 10-50x per year. Lock in long-term API contracts cautiously (prices will fall). Consider fine-tuning or training custom smaller models rather than paying for frontier API access — the cost crossover point where owning your model is cheaper than API calls is moving earlier every quarter. Build applications where value comes from data, workflow integration, or domain expertise rather than model capability alone, since model capability is rapidly commoditizing.

confidence.cross_reference: The 280x figure is reported in the Stanford HAI AI Index 2025 (https://hai.stanford.edu/ai-index/2025-ai-index-report), corroborated by Epoch AI's independent analysis (https://epoch.ai/data-insights/llm-inference-price-trends), cited by Tom's Hardware, Wing Venture Capital (who independently calculate a 240x decline for GPT-4-equivalent intelligence), and AEI. The ResNet-50 training cost decline is from ARK Invest (https://www.ark-invest.com/articles/analyst-research/ai-training), corroborated by VentureBeat reporting. Algorithmic efficiency halving time from OpenAI's 'AI and Efficiency' paper (https://openai.com/index/ai-and-efficiency/). Hardware cost data from Our World in Data (https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/hardware-and-energy-cost-to-train-notable-ai-systems).
confidence.caveats: The 280x figure specifically measures inference cost to achieve a fixed benchmark score (MMLU 64.8%), not the cost of frontier model training, which has been increasing. Benchmark performance (MMLU) is a proxy for real-world capability and may not perfectly reflect production use case improvements. The fastest decline rates (900x/year) are driven by data from the past year and may not persist. DeepSeek's $5.6M training cost claim has been debated — SemiAnalysis argues the true cost is higher when accounting for pre-training data, architecture research, and failed experiments. API pricing does not include costs of integration, prompt engineering, evaluation, and monitoring. Per-unit cost declines can be offset by increased usage volume (Jevons paradox).
confidence.measurement_reliability: analyst_estimate (training cost figures are estimates based on public compute disclosures and hardware pricing; inference costs are verifiable market prices from API providers; hardware cost per FLOP data from vendor pricing; algorithmic efficiency from controlled benchmark experiments)
